title.raw: 卷一百下 敍傳 Volume 100b: Afterword and Family History 2

sentences.zh: 卷一百下 敘傳第七十下

translations.literal: Volume 100, Part B: Afterword and Biographical Preface, Number 70, Part B
translations.idiomatic: Hanshu, volume 100b: the afterword and family history, second installment.

sentences.zh: 固以為唐虞三代，詩書所及，世有典籍，故雖堯舜之盛，必有典謨之篇，然後揚名於後世，冠德於百王，

translations.literal: Gu held that for the eras of Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties, as far as the Odes and Documents reach, the age already possessed canonical records; therefore even at the full flourishing of Yao and Shun there had to be canons and counsels in writing, and only then could they raise their fame for later ages and set their virtue above the hundred kings,
translations.idiomatic: Ban Gu argued that Yao, Shun, and the Three Ages already had written records in the classics, so even those golden reigns needed documentary canons before their virtue could tower over later kings and their memory could reach posterity.

translations.literal: 〈Yan Shigu says: "Meaning that their virtue stood above the hundred kings."〉
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu gloss: their moral prestige crowned every ruler who came after.

sentences.zh: 故曰：「巍巍乎其有成功，煥乎其有文章也！」

translations.literal: Therefore it is said, "How lofty was his success! How brilliant was his pattern!
translations.idiomatic: Hence the Analects praise Yao in those words: towering achievement, radiant culture.

sentences.zh: 〈師古曰：「此篇論語載孔子美堯舜之言也。」〉

translations.literal: 〈Yan Shigu says: "This passage records Confucius's praise of Yao and Shun in the Analects."〉
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu notes that the quotation is Confucius extolling Yao and Shun.

sentences.zh: 漢紹堯運，以建帝業，至於六世，史臣乃追述功德，私作本紀，

translations.literal: Han inherited Yao's fortune and thereby founded the imperial enterprise; down to the sixth generation the historiographers then traced meritorious deeds and privately composed basic annals,
translations.idiomatic: The Han took up Yao's mandate and built an empire; by the sixth reign court scribes looked back, chronicled the record, and drafted private "basic annals.

sentences.zh: 〈師古曰：「謂武帝時司馬遷作《史記》。」〉

translations.literal: 〈Yan Shigu says: "This refers to Sima Qian's composition of the Records of the Historian under Emperor Wu."〉
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu explains: Sima Qian wrote the Shiji during Emperor Wu's reign.

sentences.zh: 編於百王之末，廁於秦、項之列。

translations.literal: He arrayed them at the tail of the hundred kings and placed them in the same column as Qin and Xiang.
translations.idiomatic: Sima Qian filed that work after every earlier king, lumping Han with Qin and Xiang Yu.

sentences.zh: 太初以後，闕而不錄，故探篹前記，綴輯所聞，

translations.literal: After the Taichu era there were gaps and nothing was recorded; therefore I investigated and compiled earlier notes and stitched together what I had heard,
translations.idiomatic: After Taichu the thread broke; Ban Gu therefore combed older materials and pieced hearsay into a continuous narrative.

translations.literal: 〈Yan Shigu says: "Zhuan is the same as compile; ji is the same as gather."〉
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu: the word rendered zhuan here means to compile, and ji means to collect.

sentences.zh: 以述漢書，起元高祖，終于孝平王莽之誅，十有二世，二百三十年，綜其行事，旁貫五經，上下洽通，

translations.literal: in order to narrate the Book of Han, beginning with the Founding Ancestor and ending with the execution of Wang Mang under Emperor Xiaoping—twelve generations, two hundred thirty years—synthesizing their deeds, running horizontally through the Five Classics so that high and low fully interlock,
translations.idiomatic: He wrote the Hanshu from Gaozu through Wang Mang's fall—twelve reigns and two hundred thirty years—correlated events with the Five Classics, and wove the whole into one fabric.

sentences.zh: 〈師古曰：「固所撰諸表序及志，經典之義在於是也。」〉

translations.literal: 〈Yan Shigu says: "The meanings of the classics that inform Ban Gu's tables, prefaces, and treatises lie in this."〉
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu: the classical rationale behind Ban's tables, prefaces, and treatises is what this sentence claims.

sentences.zh: 為春秋考紀、表、志、傳，凡百篇。

translations.literal: making Spring-and-Autumn-style annals of investigation, tables, treatises, and traditions, in all one hundred chapters.
translations.idiomatic: He framed annals in the Spring and Autumn manner, added tables, treatises, and biographies—one hundred chapters in all.

translations.literal: 〈Yan Shigu says: "Spring-and-Autumn annals of investigation means the imperial annals.
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu begins: "Spring-and-Autumn-style annals" names the imperial annals;

sentences.zh: 而俗之學者不詳此文，乃云《漢書》一名春秋考紀，蓋失之矣。」〉

translations.literal: Yet vulgar students do not understand this text and therefore say that the Book of Han had the alternate title Spring-and-Autumn Annals of Investigation—how far they have missed the mark.〉
translations.idiomatic: Vulgar readers missed the point and invented a spurious book title, "Spring and Autumn Annals of Investigation," which is quite wrong.

translations.literal: The preface says:
translations.idiomatic: The author's summaries begin:

sentences.zh: 〈師古曰：「自『皇矣漢祖』以下諸敘，皆班固自論撰漢書意，此亦依放史記之敘目耳。

translations.literal: 〈Yan Shigu says: "From 'August indeed was the Han Founding Ancestor' downward, each summary is Ban Gu's own statement of how he meant the Hanshu to work; it follows the Shiji's table of chapter headings.
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu: from the line on Gaozu onward each "summary" is Ban Gu's statement of editorial intent, modeled on Sima Qian's chapter tags.

sentences.zh: 史遷則云為某事作某本紀、某列傳。

translations.literal: Sima Qian would say that he "composed such-and-such a basic annal" or "such-and-such a tradition.
translations.idiomatic: The Grand Historian wrote labels like "I composed the basic annal for X" or "the biography of Y.

sentences.zh: 班固謙，不言然而改言述，蓋避作者之謂聖，而取述者之謂明也。

translations.literal: Ban Gu was modest and did not say "compose" but changed it to "narrate," because he shrank from the sage's prerogative of "authoring" and took instead the clarity ascribed to one who "transmits.
translations.idiomatic: Ban Gu swapped "compose" for the humbler "narrate," avoiding the sage's claim to "make" texts while keeping the wise man's role of clarifier.

sentences.zh: 但後之學者不曉此為漢書敘目，見有述字，因謂此文追述漢書之事，乃呼為『漢書述』，失之遠矣。

translations.literal: But later students did not realize that this was the Hanshu's table of contents; seeing the word "narrate," they supposed the passage retrospectively described the Hanshu itself and dubbed it the "Narration of the Hanshu"—how wide of the mark!
translations.idiomatic: Later readers mistook these lines for a separate essay about the book and called it the "Hanshu Narration," which misses Ban's purpose entirely.

sentences.zh: 摯虞尚有此惑，其餘曷足怪乎！」〉

translations.literal: Zhi Yu still harbored this confusion; how much less surprising in others!"〉
translations.idiomatic: Even Zhi Yu fell into that error, so lesser scholars can be forgiven."

sentences.zh: 皇矣漢祖，纂堯之緒，實天生德，聰明神武。

translations.literal: August indeed was the Han Founding Ancestor: he continued Yao's thread; truly Heaven bore his virtue—acute of hearing, clear of sight, divine and martial.
translations.idiomatic: Splendid was the Han ancestor, heir to Yao's line: Heaven endowed him with keen senses and a martial, almost numinous, presence.

sentences.zh: 秦人不綱，罔漏于楚，〔一〕爰茲發跡，斷蛇奮旅。

translations.literal: Qin lost its guiding net, and the net leaked out into Chu; [note one] here he first raised his traces, cut the serpent, and roused his host.
translations.idiomatic: Qin's laws unraveled and power spilled toward Chu; there Gaozu first rose, slew the white serpent, and raised an army.

sentences.zh: 神母告符，朱旗乃舉，粵蹈秦郊，嬰來稽首。

translations.literal: The divine mother announced the token; the vermilion banner was then raised; he trod Qin's suburbs and Ying came to bow the head.
translations.idiomatic: The spirit mother proved the omen, the red flag went up, he marched on Qin's capital, and Ziying surrendered.

sentences.zh: 革命創制，三章是紀，應天順民，五星同晷。

translations.literal: He revolutionized the mandate and founded institutions; the three articles were what he recorded; he answered Heaven and followed the people; the five planets shared one gnomon shadow.
translations.idiomatic: He remade the mandate, set new laws, proclaimed the three clauses of mercy, claimed Heaven's nod and the people's heart, and watched the five planets align.

sentences.zh: 〔二〕項氏畔換，黜我巴、漢，〔三〕西土宅心，戰士憤怨。

translations.literal: [note two] The Xiang clan was arrogant and overbearing; they drove us into Ba and Han; [note three] the western lands took him as their heart; warriors nursed resentment.
translations.idiomatic: Xiang Yu bullied the realm and penned Liu Bang in Ba and Han; the west rallied to Liu while his soldiers burned for revenge.

sentences.zh: 〔四〕乘釁而運，席卷三秦，割據河山，保此懷民。

translations.literal: [note four] Riding the breach he moved his fortune, rolled up the three Qin like a mat, carved out rivers and mountains, and protected these cherishing people.
translations.idiomatic: He seized the opening, swept the three Qin, claimed the strategic ground, and shielded the people who had welcomed him.

sentences.zh: 〔五〕股肱蕭、曹，社稷是經，爪牙信、布，腹心良、平，龔行天罰，赫赫明明。

translations.literal: [note five] Thigh and arm were Xiao and Cao—they steered the altars of soil and grain; claws and fangs were Xin and Bu—belly and heart were Liang and Ping; they reverently executed Heaven's punishment, blazing and bright.
translations.idiomatic: Xiao He and Cao Shen were his arms around the state; Han Xin and Ying Bu his claws; Zhang Liang and Chen Ping his inward counsel; together they carried out Heaven's sentence in terrible splendor.

translations.literal: Narrating the Basic Annal of the High Founder, number one.
translations.idiomatic: Summary: Basic Annals of Gaozu, chapter one.

sentences.zh: 〔一〕 師古曰：「言秦失綱維，故高祖因時而起。

translations.literal: [note one] Yan Shigu says: "It means Qin lost its guiding cords, so the High Founder could rise with the times.
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu on "Qin lost its net": the First Emperor's order collapsed so Gaozu could seize the moment.

sentences.zh: 罔漏于楚，謂項羽雖有害虐之心，終免於患也。

translations.literal: The net leaking into Chu means that although Xiang Yu had a heart bent on harm and cruelty, in the end he escaped calamity."
translations.idiomatic: Another reading: "leaked to Chu" means Xiang Yu briefly held power yet never suffered Qin's fall."

sentences.zh: 一說，楚王陳涉初起，後又破滅也。」

translations.literal: Another explanation: the King of Chu Chen She first rose and afterward was destroyed as well."
translations.idiomatic: Alternatively it refers to Chen She's brief Chu uprising and swift ruin."

translations.literal: [note two] Yan Shigu says: "Gui means shadow.
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu: gui here means the gnomon's shadow—the shared alignment of the five planets.

translations.literal: [note three] Meng Kang says: "Pan means rebel.
translations.idiomatic: Meng Kang gloss: pan means to rebel.

translations.literal: Huan means change."
translations.idiomatic: Huan means to change or exchange.

sentences.zh: 不用義帝要，換易與高祖漢中也。

translations.literal: He did not use Emperor Yi's covenant but swapped Ba and Han onto the High Founder."
translations.idiomatic: He reads it as Xiang Yu breaking faith with Yi and trading Hanzhong for Liu Bang—

translations.literal: " Yan Shigu says: "This explanation is wrong.
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu rejects that gloss.

sentences.zh: 畔換，強恣之貌，猶言跋扈也。

translations.literal: Pan-huan is the appearance of violent arrogance, the same idea as hubao."
translations.idiomatic: Pan-huan means overbearing swagger, like the word hubao.

sentences.zh: 詩大雅皇矣篇曰『無然畔換』。」

translations.literal: The Greater Odes "Huangyi" piece says, "Do not be thus overbearing.
translations.idiomatic: The Greater Odes command: "Do not strut in hubris.

translations.literal: [note four] Liu De says: "Zhai means to dwell.
translations.idiomatic: Liu De: zhai means to dwell or fix the heart upon.

sentences.zh: 西方人皆居心於高祖，猶係心也。

translations.literal: All the westerners fixed their hearts on the High Founder as if tethered to him."
translations.idiomatic: Everyone west of the passes pinned hope on Gaozu as on a mooring line.

translations.literal: The Documents says, "The multitude fixed their hearts.
translations.idiomatic: The Book of Documents says the people "fixed their hearts" on the right lord.

translations.literal: " Jin Zhuo says: "Western lands means west of the passes.
translations.idiomatic: Jin Zhuo: "western lands" is the Guanzhong region.

sentences.zh: 高祖入關，約法三章，秦民大悅，皆宅心高祖。」

translations.literal: When the High Founder entered the passes and established the three articles of law, the people of Qin were greatly pleased and all fixed their hearts on the High Founder."
translations.idiomatic: When Gaozu entered with the three laws, Qin subjects rejoiced and gave him their hearts."

translations.literal: [note five] Yan Shigu says: "Bao means to settle.
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu: bao means to give security.

translations.literal: Huai-min means people cherishing virtue."
translations.idiomatic: Huai-min means folk who remember kindness.

sentences.zh: 孝惠短世，高后稱制，罔顧天顯，呂宗以敗。

translations.literal: Emperor Xiaohui's reign was short; the Empress Gao held the regent's seal; heedless of Heaven's bright way, the Lü clan thereby met ruin.
translations.idiomatic: Hui died young, Empress Lü ruled in his stead, ignored Heaven's clear pattern, and brought the Lü house to ruin.

translations.literal: [note one] Narrating the Basic Annal of Emperor Hui, number two, and the Basic Annal of Empress Gao, number three.
translations.idiomatic: Summary: Annals of Emperor Hui, chapter two; Annals of Empress Gao, chapter three.

translations.literal: [note one] Liu De says: "Wang means none.
translations.idiomatic: Liu De: wang means there was none.

translations.literal: Gu means to think on."
translations.idiomatic: Gu means to heed or bear in mind.

translations.literal: Xian means bright."
translations.idiomatic: Xian means manifest or bright.

sentences.zh: 言呂氏無念天之明道者，徒念王諸呂，以至於敗亡。」

translations.literal: It means the Lü clan never thought on Heaven's bright way but only on ennobling the Lüs as kings, and therefore reached defeat and destruction."
translations.idiomatic: The Lüs never pondered Heaven's lesson; they schemed only to crown their kin and so fell to ruin."

sentences.zh: 太宗穆穆，允恭玄默，化民以躬，帥下以德。

translations.literal: The Revered Ancestor was solemn and still, truly reverent, darkly silent; he transformed the people by his person and led those below with virtue.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Wen was grave and gentle, reverent and sparing of words; he shaped the folk by example and led officials with virtue.

sentences.zh: 農不供貢，罪不收孥，〔一〕宮不新館，陵不崇墓。

translations.literal: Farmers did not pay tribute grain; crimes did not seize wives and children; [note one] palaces built no new lodges; tombs raised no lofty mounds.
translations.idiomatic: He lifted the grain tribute, stopped punishing families for one man's crime, built no new palace halls, and piled no extravagant tombs.

sentences.zh: 〔二〕我德如風，民應如屮，〔三〕國富刑清，登我漢道。

translations.literal: [note two] My virtue was like the wind; the people's response was like grass; [note three] the state grew rich, punishments grew clear, and we ascended the Han Way.
translations.idiomatic: His virtue was wind, the people grass bending with it; wealth rose, justice cleared, and the Han road climbed toward good order.

translations.literal: [note four] Narrating the Basic Annal of the Cultured Emperor, number four.
translations.idiomatic: Summary: Annals of Emperor Wen, chapter four.

sentences.zh: 〔一〕 張晏曰：「除民田租之稅，是不供貢也。」

translations.literal: [note one] Zhang Yan says: "He removed the field-land tax—that is what not supplying tribute means.
translations.idiomatic: Zhang Yan: ending the land tax is the sense of "farmers paid no tribute.

translations.literal: [note two] Yan Shigu says: "For rhyme mu is read like mo.
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu notes the poem rhymes the word for tomb as mo.

sentences.zh: 〔三〕 師古曰：「論語稱孔子曰：『君子之德風，小人之德屮也。

translations.literal: [note three] Yan Shigu says: "The Analects records Confucius saying, 'The gentleman's virtue is wind; the small man's virtue is grass.
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu cites the Analects: the gentleman's virtue is wind, the commoner's grass.

translations.literal: Therefore he quoted it as his wording."
translations.idiomatic: Ban Gu borrows Confucius's image for Wen's reign."

translations.literal: [note four] Yan Shigu says: "Deng means to complete.
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu: deng here means to complete or bring to fulfillment.

sentences.zh: 孝景蒞政，諸侯方命，〔一〕克伐七國，王室以定。

translations.literal: Emperor Xiaojing took the reins; the feudal lords defied their charge; [note one] he conquered and struck down the seven states, and the royal house was thereby settled.
translations.idiomatic: Jingdi faced defiant kingdoms, crushed the seven-state revolt, and secured the throne.

sentences.zh: 匪怠匪荒，務在農桑，著于甲令，民用寧康。

translations.literal: Neither slack nor wasteful, he pressed agriculture and sericulture; he set it in the ordinances of the first month, and the people used it to find peace.
translations.idiomatic: Neither lazy nor reckless, he pushed farming and silk work, codified it in first-month edicts, and the people lived at ease.

translations.literal: [note two] Narrating the Basic Annal of the Accomplished Emperor, number five.
translations.idiomatic: Summary: Annals of Emperor Jing, chapter five.

sentences.zh: 〔一〕 孟康曰：「尚書云『方命圮族』，言鯀之惡，壞其族類。

translations.literal: [note one] Meng Kang says: "The Documents says 'defying the charge he ruined his kin'—it speaks of Gun's evil and destroying his kindred.
translations.idiomatic: Meng Kang: "defying the charge" echoes the Documents on Gun ruining his clan.

translations.literal: The seven states of Wu and Chu were the same."
translations.idiomatic: The seven kingdoms behaved like Gun."

sentences.zh: 〔二〕 師古曰：「甲令，即景紀令甲也。」

translations.literal: [note two] Yan Shigu says: "Jia-ling means the first-month ordinances recorded in Jingdi's annals.
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu: jia-ling refers to the ordinances cited in Jing's annals.

sentences.zh: 世宗曄曄，思弘祖業，〔一〕疇咨熙載，髦俊並作。

translations.literal: The World Ancestor blazed bright, thinking to enlarge the Founder's enterprise; [note one] he asked who could help lift the glorious burden, and splendid talents rose together.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Wu shone with ambition to widen Gaozu's work; he sought who could shoulder the bright task, and brilliant men rose beside him.

translations.literal: [note two] What did their work become?
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu unpacks the next line: what did they accomplish?

sentences.zh: 百蠻是攘，〔三〕恢我疆宇，外博四荒。

translations.literal: The hundred barbarians were driven back; [note three] he widened our borders and broadened the four wilds without.
translations.idiomatic: They beat back the barbarians, widened the frontiers, and pushed power into the four wastes.

sentences.zh: 〔四〕武功既抗，亦迪斯文，〔五〕憲章六學，統壹聖真。

translations.literal: [note four] Military prowess once established, he also advanced this pattern of culture; [note five] he took the six arts as his charter and unified the sage's truth.
translations.idiomatic: Arms secured, he advanced culture, modeled the six classics, and gathered the sage's teaching into one.

translations.literal: He feng and shan sacrificed at the suburbs and ranked the hundred spirits;
translations.idiomatic: He offered the fengshan rites, worshiped heaven and earth, and ordered the pantheon;

translations.literal: harmonized pitch pipes and corrected the calendar, feasting thereby on long years.
translations.idiomatic: set the pitch pipes and calendar right, and sought long life through ordered ritual.

translations.literal: [note six] Narrating the Basic Annal of the Martial Emperor, number six.
translations.idiomatic: Summary: Annals of Emperor Wu, chapter six.

translations.literal: [note one] Yan Shigu says: "Ye-ye describes a flourishing appearance.
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu: ye-ye means radiant, in full flourish.

translations.literal: [note two] Yan Shigu says: "Chou means who.
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu: chou means who,

translations.literal: Zi means counsel.
translations.idiomatic: Zi means to consult,

translations.literal: Xi means to raise up.
translations.idiomatic: Xi means to brighten or uplift,

translations.literal: Zai means affair.
translations.idiomatic: Zai means task or undertaking.

translations.literal: He consulted the assembled worthies: who
translations.idiomatic: He asked his wise ministers who

translations.literal: (could)
translations.idiomatic: (could)

translations.literal: [worthy of] appointment, and therefore could raise his enterprises.
translations.idiomatic: Might be trusted with office and so lift the great enterprise.

translations.literal: Zuo means to begin.
translations.idiomatic: Zuo means to initiate or arise.

translations.literal: [note three] Yan Shigu says: "Rang means to thrust back.
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu: rang means to repel or push aside.

translations.literal: [note four] Yan Shigu says: "Hui means to widen.
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu: hui means to extend or broaden.

translations.literal: Bo means great.
translations.idiomatic: Bo means vast or great.

translations.literal: [note five] Liu De says: "Di means to advance.
translations.idiomatic: Liu De: di means to promote or advance.

sentences.zh: 〔六〕 張晏曰：「改正謂從建寅之月也。」

translations.literal: [note six] Zhang Yan says: "Correcting the calendar means taking the first month as the jianyin month.
translations.idiomatic: Zhang Yan: "correcting the calendar" means adopting the jianyin new year.

translations.literal: Emperor Xiaozhao was young; the grand steward was loyal.
translations.idiomatic: Zhaodi was a child; Huo Guang as regent stayed faithful.

sentences.zh: 燕、蓋譸張，實叡實聰，〔一〕罪人斯得，邦家和同。

translations.literal: Yan and Gai swaggered and deceived; [note one] he was truly keen and truly perceptive; the guilty were then caught, and the state and families were harmonized.
translations.idiomatic: The Yan and Gai cabals blustered and lied, yet the boy emperor proved shrewd, criminals fell, and the court found peace.

translations.literal: Narrating the Basic Annal of Emperor Zhao, number seven.
translations.idiomatic: Summary: Annals of Emperor Zhao, chapter seven.

translations.literal: [note one] Ru Chun says: "Zhou is read like the word for carriage-pole (zhou).
translations.idiomatic: Ru Chun: pronounce the first syllable of zhou-zhang like the word for a chariot pole.

translations.literal: " Ying Shao says: "Zhou-zhang means deception."
translations.idiomatic: Ying Shao: zhou-zhang means deceit or boasting.

sentences.zh: 中宗明明，夤用刑名，〔一〕時舉傅納，聽斷惟精。

translations.literal: The Middle Ancestor was enlightened and clear, reverently using punishments and names; [note one] he timely raised men and accepted counsel; in hearing cases and deciding suits he was utterly precise.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Xuan was lucid and careful with law and administrative labels; he promoted talent, listened to advice, and judged lawsuits with exact care.

sentences.zh: 〔二〕柔遠能邇，燀燿威靈，〔三〕龍荒幕朔，莫不來庭。

translations.literal: [note two] He softened those far and strengthened those near, blazing with awesome numen; [note three] from the dragon wastes to the desert north, none failed to come to court.
translations.idiomatic: He soothed distant tribes and knit the heartland, his majesty blazing so that border peoples all came to audience.

translations.literal: [note four] Greatly manifesting the Founder's blazing deeds, he honored those who had achieved success.
translations.idiomatic: He displayed Gaozu's legacy and honored men of real achievement.

translations.literal: [note five] Narrating the Basic Annal of Emperor Xuan, number eight.
translations.idiomatic: Summary: Annals of Emperor Xuan, chapter eight.

translations.literal: [note one] Deng Zhan says: "Yin means reverent.
translations.idiomatic: Deng Zhan: yin means reverent or scrupulous.

translations.literal: [note two] Li Qi says: "Shi means this or that moment.
translations.idiomatic: Li Qi: shi means at this time or right then.

translations.literal: At this time he selected and employed worthy men.

translations.idiomatic: Note 2: the compiler keeps the main framework to unify the inherited wording.

translations.literal: Narrating the Treatise on Rites and Music, second.
translations.idiomatic: Summation of the treatise on rites and music—the second in the series.

sentences.zh: 〔一〕 劉德曰：「兌下乾上履，坤下震上豫。

translations.literal: [1] Liu De says: "Below dui, qian above is Li; below kun, zhen above is Yu.
translations.idiomatic: Liu De, note 1: the hexagrams are Li, with marsh below and heaven above, and Yu, with earth below and thunder above.

translations.literal: Li means rites.
translations.idiomatic: "Li" signifies ritual propriety.

translations.literal: Yu means music.
translations.idiomatic: "Yu" signifies music and dance.

translations.literal: They drew on the Changes' images to establish rites and create music.
translations.idiomatic: From those Classic of Changes emblems the sages derived ceremonial forms and musical composition.

sentences.zh: 」師古曰：「易象曰『上天下澤履，雷出地奮豫』，故具引其文。」

translations.literal: " Yan Shigu says: "The Image text states 'Heaven above marsh—Li; thunder emerging from the earth—Yu,' hence he quotes it in full."
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu cites the standard Image commentary on Li and Yu as Ban Gu's source.

sentences.zh: 〔二〕 師古曰：「言上風既流，下人則化也。

translations.literal: [2] Yan Shigu says: "It means that when the airs above had drifted downward, the people below were transformed.
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu, note 2: popular song reshaped the common people once it spread from above.

translations.literal: Mianmian means drifting and shifting.
translations.idiomatic: "Mianmian" describes a current that carries people along.

translations.literal: Fenfen means mixed disorder.
translations.idiomatic: "Fenfen" means tangled confusion.

translations.literal: Mian is read mo-jian fan."
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu gives the fanqie reading for "mian."

sentences.zh: 靁電皆至，天威震耀，五刑之作，是則是效，〔一〕威實輔德，刑亦助教。

translations.literal: Thunder and lightning both arrive; heaven's majesty shakes and dazzles; the five punishments were instituted—thus they were taken as models; awe truly assists virtue, and punishments likewise aid instruction.
translations.idiomatic: Lightning and thunder manifest celestial authority; the five punishments were framed as models because terror reinforces moral sway even as penal law supports teaching.

sentences.zh: 季世不詳，背本爭末，〔二〕吳、孫狙詐，申、商酷烈。

translations.literal: In a decadent age they did not exhaust the principle; they turned their backs on the root and contended over the twigs; [2] Wu and Sun practiced deceit; Shen Buhai and Shang Yang were harsh in the extreme.
translations.idiomatic: Late ages mishandled justice, chasing expedients over fundamentals; the strategists of Wu and Sun turned to cunning, while the legalists Shen Buhai and Shang Yang enforced pitiless severity.

sentences.zh: 〔三〕漢章九法，太宗改作，〔四〕輕重之差，世有定籍。

translations.literal: [3] Han set forth its nine articles of law; the Grand Ancestor revised the code; [4] the gradations of severity and leniency came to rest in fixed statutes generation after generation.
translations.idiomatic: Note 3: the Han promulgated its nine legal canons; note 4: Emperor Wen remade the system, and thereafter the scales of punishment were recorded in stable codes.

translations.literal: Narrating the Treatise on Punishments and Law, third.
translations.idiomatic: Summation of the treatise on penal law—the third in the series.

sentences.zh: 〔一〕 劉德曰：「震下離上，噬嗑，利用獄。

translations.literal: [1] Liu De says: "Below zhen, li above—Shike, beneficial to employ punishments.
translations.idiomatic: Liu De, note 1: the hexagram Shi Ke (Biting Through), thunder below and fire above, is favorable for employing punishments; its thunder-and-lightning image stands for heaven's awesome authority.

translations.literal: Thunder and lightning take the image of heaven's majesty.
translations.idiomatic: The storm emblems stand for celestial terror applied to judgment.

sentences.zh: 」師古曰：「易象辭曰『雷電，噬嗑，先王以明罰敕法』，故引之。」

translations.literal: " Yan Shigu says: "The Image text reads 'Thunder and lightning—Shike; the former kings clarified penalties and admonished the laws,' hence he cites it."
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu quotes the Changes' Image on Shike as the textual basis.

sentences.zh: 〔二〕 師古曰：「不詳謂不盡用刑之理也。

translations.literal: [2] Yan Shigu says: "Bu xiang means they did not exhaust the rationale of punishment.
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu, note 2: "bu xiang" indicates failure to apply penal theory thoroughly.

translations.literal: The Zhou document "Lu Xing" says, 'I tell you to exhaustively apply punishments.'"
translations.idiomatic: He parallels the phrase to the "Lu Xing" injunction to judge with full deliberation.

translations.literal: [3] Yan Shigu says: "Ju is read qian-yu fan."
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu, note 3: fanqie pronunciation for "ju" (cunning).

translations.literal: [4] Zhang Yan says: "Gai means abolishing the mutilating punishments."
translations.idiomatic: Zhang Yan, note 4: the revision refers to ending flesh penalties under Emperor Wen.

translations.literal: From the first birth of the people, food and goods have come first.
translations.idiomatic: For humankind since its beginnings, subsistence and exchange have been the foundation.

sentences.zh: 割制廬井，定爾土田，什一供貢，下富上尊。

translations.literal: They carved out well-and-field hamlets, fixed your soil and fields, took one-tenth in tribute, and thereby the low grew rich while the high remained honored.
translations.idiomatic: The well-field grid apportioned farmland, fixed the tithe at one tenth, and secured prosperity below while dignity stayed with the throne.

sentences.zh: 商以足用，茂遷有無，貨自龜貝，至此五銖。

translations.literal: Trade made supplies sufficient; vigorous exchange moved surplus and want; currency began with tortoise shells and cowries down to the present five-zhu coin.
translations.idiomatic: Commerce balanced supply; circulation matched abundance to need; money evolved from shells and cowries to the Han five-zhu piece.

translations.literal: They weighed past and present and watched the world's fullness and emptiness.
translations.idiomatic: The treatise surveys antiquity and the present to read the economy's ebbs and flows.

translations.literal: [1] Narrating the Treatise on Food and Money, fourth.
translations.idiomatic: Note 1: summation of the treatise on food and currency—the fourth in the series.

translations.literal: [1] Yan Shigu says: "Yang means to raise.
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu, note 1: "yang" is "to lift up."

translations.literal: Que means to draw out.
translations.idiomatic: "Que" means to draw forth or extend.

sentences.zh: 揚搉者，舉而引之，陳其趣也。

translations.literal: Yang-que means to raise and draw out, setting forth the drift of the argument.
translations.idiomatic: "Yang-que" is a compound for laying out the argument's direction.

translations.literal: Que is read ju-xue fan."
translations.idiomatic: He gives the fanqie reading for "que."

sentences.zh: 昔在上聖，昭事百神，類帝禋宗，望秩山川，明德惟馨，永世豐年。

translations.literal: In antiquity the supreme sages brightly served the hundred spirits; they classified the Lord on High and performed yin sacrifice at the ancestral temple; they offered the ranked sacrifices to mountains and rivers; illustrious virtue was the fragrance, and age after age enjoyed abundant harvests.
translations.idiomatic: The greatest sage-kings worshipped the host of deities, sacrificed to Heaven and Earth, and offered the ordered oblations to mountains and rivers, so their luminous virtue brought lasting plenty.

sentences.zh: 季末淫祀，營信巫史，〔一〕大夫臚岱，侯伯僭畤，〔二〕放誕之徒，緣間而起。

translations.literal: At the end of an age licentious cults multiplied; people trusted shamans and scribes; [1] great officers staged the Tai offering; marquises and earls presumptuously set up suburban altars; [2] reckless men seized the opening and rose on it.
translations.idiomatic: Decadent eras drowned in irregular worship, credulous of mediums and clerks; nobles usurped the imperial sacrifice at Mount Tai while lords raised illicit suburban shrines, and charlatans rushed into the breach.

translations.literal: [3] Looking before and behind, I set right their beginnings and ends.
translations.idiomatic: Note 3: the treatise surveys the full arc to correct the record from start to finish.

translations.literal: Narrating the Treatise on Suburban Sacrifices, fifth.
translations.idiomatic: Summation of the treatise on suburban sacrifices—the fifth in the series.

translations.literal: [1] Deng Zhan says: "Ying means deluded."
translations.idiomatic: Deng Zhan, note 1: "ying" here means "misled" or "bewitched."

sentences.zh: 〔二〕 鄭氏曰：「臚岱，季氏旅於太山是也。

translations.literal: [2] Zheng shi says: "Lu Dai refers to the Ji clan's 'journey' (lu) at Mount Tai.
translations.idiomatic: Zheng's gloss, note 2: "lu Dai" is the Ji family's unauthorized grand offering at Taishan.

translations.idiomatic: Ying Shao continues: usurping the suburban altar means Duke Wen of Qin founded

translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu: "lu" means to set forth in array.

translations.idiomatic: "Lu" likewise means "to display" or "marshal."

translations.literal: The sounds of lu and lu are close; their sense is one."
translations.idiomatic: The two words sound alike and carry the same meaning here.

sentences.zh: 〔三〕 師古曰：「謂方士言神仙之術也。」

translations.literal: [3] Yan Shigu says: "It refers to the fangshi speaking of the arts of immortals."
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu, note 3: the allusion is to occultists promising transcendence.

sentences.zh: 炫炫上天，縣象著明，〔一〕日月周輝，星辰垂精。

translations.literal: Dazzling heaven above, suspended images shine clear; [1] sun and moon wheel their radiance; the stars hang down their essence.
translations.idiomatic: Brilliant heaven displays its hanging patterns: the luminaries revolve while constellations shed their influence below.

sentences.zh: 百官立法，宮室混成，〔二〕降應王政，景以燭形。

translations.literal: The hundred offices set laws; palace chambers took harmonious form; [2] they lowered responses to the king's government, and the shadow-stick mirrored the body.
translations.idiomatic: Bureaucratic regulations matched celestial mansions; royal policy drew answering signs from the sky as a shadow reproduces a form.

sentences.zh: 〔三〕三季之後，厥事放紛，〔四〕舉其占應，覽故考新。

translations.literal: [3] After the three final ages, those affairs grew scattered and confused; [4] I lift their prognostications and responses, scanning the old and testing the new.
translations.idiomatic: Note 3: after the three dynasties' twilight, astral lore grew chaotic; note 4: the treatise collects omens old and new for comparison.

translations.literal: Narrating the Treatise on Astronomy, sixth.
translations.idiomatic: Summation of the treatise on astronomy—the sixth in the series.

sentences.zh: 〔一〕 師古曰：「炫炫，光耀之貌，音胡眄反。

translations.literal: [1] Yan Shigu says: "Xuanxuan describes a shining appearance, read hu-mian fan.
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu, note 1: "xuanxuan" means radiant; he gives the fanqie reading.

translations.literal: Xian is the ancient character for xuan 'suspend'."
translations.idiomatic: "Xian" is the old graph for the character meaning "to suspend" or "hang aloft."

sentences.zh: 〔二〕 張晏曰：「星辰有宮室百官，各應其象以見咎徵也。」

translations.literal: [2] Zhang Yan says: "The stars have palaces and the hundred offices; each corresponds to its image to show blame and warning."
translations.idiomatic: Zhang Yan, note 2: constellations are mapped to government posts to portend fault.

sentences.zh: 〔三〕 張晏曰：「王政失於此，星辰變於彼，猶景之象形。」

translations.literal: [3] Zhang Yan says: "Where the king's government failed here, the stars changed there—just as a shadow matches a body."
translations.idiomatic: Zhang Yan, note 3: celestial anomalies answer terrestrial misrule like shadow to substance.

sentences.zh: 〔四〕 師古曰：「三季，三代之末也。

translations.literal: [4] Yan Shigu says: "The three final ages are the ends of the three dynasties.
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu, note 4: the three "final ages" are the closing phases of Xia, Shang, and Zhou.

translations.literal: Fang means lost.
translations.idiomatic: "Fang" means "to slip" or "lose proper course."

translations.literal: Fen means disorder."
translations.idiomatic: "Fen" means confusion or chaos.

sentences.zh: 河圖命庖，洛書賜禹，八卦成列，九疇逌敘。

translations.literal: The River Chart commanded Pao; the Luo Document was granted to Yu; the eight trigrams formed their rows; the nine divisions followed in orderly sequence.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven revealed the River Chart to Fuxi and the Luo Writing to Yu; from them the eight trigrams and the nine fields of the "Great Plan" took ordered shape.

sentences.zh: 〔一〕世代寔寶，光演文武，春秋之占，咎徵是舉。

translations.literal: [1] Age after age they were true treasures; their light spread King Wen and King Wu; the prognostications of the Spring and Autumn period raised these signs of blame.
translations.idiomatic: Note 1: later ages treasured these patterns; they illumined the Zhou founders; Spring and Autumn annals teem with such portents.

translations.literal: They inform us of the past so we may know what comes; they are the surface of royal affairs.
translations.idiomatic: They let one read yesterday to foresee tomorrow—the public face of kingship.

translations.literal: Narrating the Treatise on the Five Phases, seventh.
translations.idiomatic: Summation of the treatise on the five phases—the seventh in the series.

sentences.zh: 〔一〕 李奇曰：「河圖即八卦也。

translations.literal: [1] Li Qi says: "The River Chart is the eight trigrams.
translations.idiomatic: Li Qi, note 1: the River Chart embodies the eight trigrams.

translations.literal: The Luo Document is the nine divisions of the "Great Plan."
translations.idiomatic: The Luo Writing corresponds to the "Hong fan" nine categories.

translations.literal: " Yan Shigu says: "Pao means Pao Xi (Fuxi).
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu: "Pao" is Fuxi.

translations.literal: You is the ancient character for you 攸."
translations.idiomatic: "You" again is the archaic form of the character read you in the sense of "thereupon."

sentences.zh: 坤作墬勢，高下九則，〔一〕自昔黃、唐，經略萬國，

translations.literal: Kun forms the configuration of the earth; high and low follow the nine grades; [1] from antiquity the Yellow Lord and Tang
translations.idiomatic: The "earth" hexagram image sorts terrain into nine ranks; since high antiquity the Yellow Emperor and Tang

translations.idiomatic: The manuscript marks an editorial lacuna with "(bian)"—likely a damaged character in the source.

translations.literal: [Xie] fixed east and west, delimited south and north.
translations.idiomatic: Note "Xie": they harmonized the compass points and drew the cardinal boundaries.

sentences.zh: 〔二〕三代損益，降及秦、漢，革剗五等，制立郡縣。

translations.literal: [2] The three dynasties increased or reduced the system; down to Qin and Han they scraped away the five ranks and established commanderies and counties.
translations.idiomatic: Note 2: Xia, Shang, and Zhou adjusted feudal grades; by Qin and Han the five-tier nobility gave way to a grid of commanderies and counties.

translations.literal: [3] I sketch the mountains and rivers to display how the land was carved apart.
translations.idiomatic: Note 3: a schematic geography shows how the realm was partitioned.

translations.literal: Narrating the Treatise on Geography, eighth.
translations.idiomatic: Summation of the treatise on geography—the eighth in the series.

translations.literal: [1] Zhang Yan says: "The Changes reads 'The configuration of the earth is kun.'
translations.idiomatic: Zhang Yan, note 1: quoting "The earth's power is kun" from the classic.

sentences.zh: 」劉德曰：「九則，九州土田上中下九等也。

translations.literal: " Liu De says: "The nine grades are the nine classes of soil quality in the nine provinces.
translations.idiomatic: Liu De: the "nine grades" are the ninefold ranking of soils across the nine regions.

translations.literal: " Yan Shigu says: "Di is the ancient character for earth.
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu: "di" is the old form of "earth."

sentences.zh: 易象曰：『地勢坤，君子以厚德載物。

translations.literal: The Image text says: 'The configuration of the earth is kun; the nobleman thereby thickens virtue and carries all things.
translations.idiomatic: He cites the Image: the nobleman thickens character and bears all things like the receptive earth.

translations.literal: ' High and low refer to landforms.
translations.idiomatic: High and low here describe physical relief.

translations.literal: Another reading: the fertility or barrenness of the soil."
translations.idiomatic: Alternatively the phrase grades fertile against poor soil.

translations.idiomatic: "Jiang-li" is setting borders and administering within them.

sentences.zh: 〔三〕 晉灼曰：「剗音剗削之剗。

translations.literal: [3] Jin Zhuo says: "Chan is read like the chan in chan-xue (to plane).
translations.idiomatic: Jin Zhuo, note 3: "chan" parallels the verb "to plane away."

translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu supplies the fanqie reading for "chan."

translations.literal: Xia rode the four conveyances; the hundred streams were guided.
translations.idiomatic: Yu of Xia toured on the four vehicles while every channel was brought under control.

translations.literal: [1] Only the Yellow River remained difficult; disaster reached later generations.
translations.idiomatic: Note 1: the Yellow River alone stayed intractable, bequeathing calamity to ages that followed.

sentences.zh: 商竭周移，秦決南涯，〔二〕自茲拒漢，北亡八支。

translations.literal: Shang exhausted it and Zhou shifted it; Qin cut through the southern bank; [2] from then on opposing the Han, the north lost eight branches.
translations.idiomatic: Shang drained its force and Zhou diverted it; Qin breached the south levee; note 2: thereafter, resisting Han control, the northern distributaries lost eight channels.

sentences.zh: 〔三〕文陻棗野，武作瓠歌，〔四〕成有平年，後遂滂沱。

translations.literal: [3] Emperor Wen penned a lament for drowned jujube groves; Emperor Wu composed the Gourd song; [4] Cheng enjoyed a peaceful year, but afterward it swelled into flood.
translations.idiomatic: Note 3: Wen mourned the inundation at Zaoye; note 4: Wu celebrated partial success in verse, yet under Cheng calm years gave way again to vast floods.

translations.literal: [5] Down to ditches and canals, they benefited our state.
translations.idiomatic: Note 5: the record extends to irrigation works that strengthened the realm.

translations.literal: Narrating the Treatise on Ditches and Conduits, ninth.
translations.idiomatic: Summation of the treatise on hydraulics—the ninth in the series.

sentences.zh: 〔一〕 師古曰：「四載，解在溝洫志。」

translations.literal: [1] Yan Shigu says: "The four conveyances are explained in the Treatise on Ditches and Conduits."
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu, note 1: the gloss on Yu's four vehicles belongs in the hydraulics treatise.

translations.literal: [2] Fu Qian says: "When the Yellow River dried up, Shang perished.
translations.idiomatic: Fu Qian, note 2: a parched riverbed foretold Shang's fall.

translations.idiomatic: "Yi" here means the channel migrated.

translations.idiomatic: Ru Chun adds Qin's deliberate cut that drowned Daliang and linked the floodwaters into the Huai-Si network.

sentences.zh: 〔三〕 服虔曰：「本有九河，今塞，餘有一也。」

translations.literal: [3] Fu Qian says: "Originally there were nine branches of the river; now they are blocked, and only one remains."
translations.idiomatic: Fu Qian, note 3: the legendary nine distributaries have silted up until a single course survives.

translations.literal: [4] Fu Qian says: "Yin is read like the yin in 'cause' (phonetic gloss).
translations.idiomatic: Fu Qian, note 4: the character for the embankment is glossed by sound.

translations.literal: Emperor Wen dammed the river at Suanzao.
translations.idiomatic: Wendi's emergency works blocked the breach near Suanzao.

sentences.zh: 」張晏曰：「河決瓠子，武帝親臨，悼功不成而作歌。」

translations.literal: " Zhang Yan says: "The river burst at Huzi; Emperor Wu went in person, mourned the unfinished work, and composed a song."
translations.idiomatic: Zhang Yan recalls Wudi's vigil at Huzi and the lament he wrote when the project stalled.

sentences.zh: 〔五〕 劉德曰：「成帝治河已平，改元曰河平元年。」

translations.literal: [5] Liu De says: "After Emperor Cheng had the river works brought under control, he changed the era name to the first year of Heping."
translations.idiomatic: Liu De, note 5: Chengdi renamed the reign to mark the year the floodplain was finally pacified.

sentences.zh: 虙羲畫卦，書契後作，〔一〕虞夏商周，孔纂其業，篹書刪詩，綴禮正樂，〔二〕彖系大易，因史立法。

translations.literal: Fuxi drew the trigrams; tallies and contracts came afterward; [1] through Yu, Xia, Shang, and Zhou, Confucius continued the enterprise—he compiled the Documents, pruned the Odes, linked the Rites, and set the music straight; [2] he appended the "Wings" to the Great Changes and founded penal models on the histories.
translations.idiomatic: From Fuxi's hexagrams to written records, then through the classical dynasties, the Master consolidated the canon: editing scripture and song, aligning ritual and pitch, commenting the Changes, and shaping law from the annals.

sentences.zh: 〔三〕六學既登，遭世罔弘，〔四〕群言紛亂，諸子相騰。

translations.literal: [3] Once the six arts had been established, they met an age unable to magnify them; [4] contending voices tangled, and the masters galloped against one another.
translations.idiomatic: Note 3: the six classical disciplines had taken shape; note 4: the late Zhou could not sustain them, and rival schools shouted past each other.

sentences.zh: 〔五〕秦人是滅，漢修其缺，劉向司籍，九流以別。

translations.literal: [5] The people of Qin extinguished that learning; the Han repaired what was missing; Liu Xiang took charge of the archives, and the nine currents were sorted apart.
translations.idiomatic: Note 5: Qin's purge scattered the texts; Han restoration brought Liu Xiang to catalogue the shelves and separate the nine intellectual lineages.

translations.literal: [6] Thereupon he set down a catalogue and briefly narrated their great achievements.
translations.idiomatic: Note 6: from that catalogue Ban Gu sketches each school's legacy.

translations.literal: [7] Narrating the Treatise on Literature, tenth.
translations.idiomatic: Note 7: summation of the bibliographic treatise—the tenth in the series.

translations.literal: [1] Yan Shigu says: "Fu is read the same as Fu (the surname Fuxi)."
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu, note 1: the archaic name Fuxi uses the "Fu" pronunciation.

translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu, note 2: "zuan" here means editorial compilation.

sentences.zh: 〔三〕 師古曰：「謂修春秋定帝王之文。」

translations.literal: [3] Yan Shigu says: "It refers to revising the Spring and Autumn Annals and fixing the canonical wording of emperors and kings."
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu, note 3: the phrase points to Confucius's editorial work on the chronicle.

translations.literal: [4] Yan Shigu says: "Wang means 'none.'
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu, note 4: "wang" negates possibility.

translations.literal: There was none who could enlarge the great Way."
translations.idiomatic: No ruler of the time could expand the true kingly teaching.

translations.literal: [5] Yan Shigu says: "Teng means to gallop."
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu, note 5: "teng" is "to race" or "surge forward."

sentences.zh: 〔六〕 應劭曰：「儒、道、陰陽、法、名、墨、從橫、雜、農，凡九家。」

translations.literal: [6] Ying Shao says: "Confucians, Daoists, yin-yang theorists, legalists, logicians, Mohists, coalition advisers, syncretists, and agrarians—nine schools in all."
translations.idiomatic: Ying Shao, note 6: the ninefold classification of Warring States philosophy.

translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu, note 2: former friends became mutual predators.

sentences.zh: 三枿之起，本根既朽，〔一〕枯楊生華，曷惟其舊！

translations.literal: When the three stumps sprouted, the root was already rotten; [1] a withered poplar puts forth blossoms—how can it long remain what it was?
translations.idiomatic: Ban Gu compares reviving rebel houses to shoots from a felled tree—flashy but unsustainable.

sentences.zh: 〔二〕橫雖雄材，伏于海隝，沐浴尸鄉，北面奉首，旅人慕殉，義過黃鳥。

translations.literal: [2] Although Tian Heng was a hero of his age, he hid on a sea island, bathed himself at Shi village, and presented his head to the north; wayfarers admired those who died with him, and their righteousness surpassed the tale of the yellow birds.
translations.idiomatic: Note 2: Tian Heng's last stand, ritual suicide, and the retainers who followed him outdo even the moral of the ode on forced burial.

translations.literal: [3] Narrating the Biographies of Wei Bao, Tian Dan, and Han Xin, third.
translations.idiomatic: Note 3: summation of the third grouped biography—Wei Bao, Tian Dan, and Han Xin.

sentences.zh: 〔一〕 劉德曰：「詩云『包有三枿』。

translations.idiomatic: Liu De, note 1: he cites the Shijing image of new shoots from a stump.

translations.literal: The Erya reads 'lie and nie mean a remainder.'
translations.idiomatic: The Erya glosses "nie" as leftover growth.

translations.literal: It means a tree shorn to the stump yet sprouting again.
translations.idiomatic: The figure is timber cut flush that still sends up suckers.

sentences.zh: 喻魏、齊、韓皆滅而復起，若髡木更生也。

translations.literal: It likens Wei, Qi, and Han—all extinguished yet rising again—to a shaved tree putting forth new life.
translations.idiomatic: Wei, Qi, and Han had fallen yet reappeared, like coppiced elms.

translations.literal: " Yan Shigu says: "Nie is read wu-ge fan."
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu supplies the fanqie reading for "nie."

sentences.zh: 〔二〕 應劭曰：「易云『枯楊生華』，暫貴之意也。

translations.literal: [2] Ying Shao says: "The Changes says 'the withered poplar puts forth blossoms,' meaning a fleeting honor.
translations.idiomatic: Ying Shao, note 2: the hexagram line speaks of brief, deceptive prosperity.

translations.literal: He wei qi jiu asks how it can stay the same as of old—it cannot last long.
translations.idiomatic: "How can it match its former state?" implies imminent collapse.

sentences.zh: 」師古曰：「枯楊生華，大過卦九五爻辭也。

translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu identifies the line as Da guo, line five.

translations.idiomatic: He notes the rhyme reading for "jiu."

sentences.zh: 〔三〕 劉德曰：「黃鳥之詩刺秦穆公要人從死，言今橫不要而有從者，故曰過之。」

translations.literal: [3] Liu De says: "The ode 'Yellow Birds' rebukes Duke Mu of Qin for forcing people to follow him in death; here Tian Heng never demanded companions yet retainers followed—so their deed surpasses the ode."
translations.idiomatic: Liu De, note 3: voluntary martyrdom outshines the forced suicides lamented in the Shijing.

sentences.zh: 信惟餓隸，布實黥徒，越亦狗盜，芮尹江湖。

translations.literal: Han Xin was only a famished underling; Bu was in truth a tattooed convict; Yue was likewise a dog-thief; Rui served as magistrate over the rivers and lakes.
translations.idiomatic: The stanza catalogues low origins: Han Xin a starving retainer, Ying Bu a branded felon, Peng Yue a common bandit, Wu Rui a magistrate amid the Yangzi lakes.

sentences.zh: 〔一〕雲起龍襄，化為侯王，〔二〕割有齊、楚，跨制淮、梁。

translations.literal: [1] Clouds rose and the dragon lifted—they turned into marquises and kings; [2] they carved out Qi and Chu and spanned the Huai and Liang regions.
translations.idiomatic: Note 1: from obscurity they soared to feudal rank; note 2: their domains stretched from the Central Plain to the Huai and Liang.

sentences.zh: 〔三〕綰自同閈，鎮我北疆，〔四〕德薄位尊，非胙惟殃。

translations.literal: [3] Wan shared the same ward gateway and guarded our northern frontier; [4] thin virtue paired with exalted rank brought not fiefs but disaster.
translations.idiomatic: Note 3: Lu Wan's neighborhood tie to Gaozu won him the Yan frontier; note 4: unmerited elevation courted ruin.

translations.literal: Wu Rui proved loyal and true, and his line therefore endured long.
translations.idiomatic: Only Wu Rui's house kept faith, so its heirs survived.

translations.literal: Narrating the Biographies of Han Xin, Peng Yue, Ying Bu, Lu Wan, and Wu Rui, fourth.
translations.idiomatic: Summation of the fourth grouped biography—the enfeoffed generals and Wu Rui.

sentences.zh: 〔一〕 張晏曰：「吳芮為番陽令，在江湖之間。

translations.idiomatic: Zhang Yan, note 1: Wu Rui governed the lake-and-river country.

translations.literal: Yin means 'to preside over.'"
translations.idiomatic: "Yin" here means he administered the region.

translations.literal: [2] Yan Shigu says: "Xiang means 'to raise aloft.'"
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu, note 2: "xiang" is "to lift" or "exalt."

sentences.zh: 〔三〕 張晏曰：「韓信前王齊，徙楚。

translations.idiomatic: Zhang Yan, note 3: Han Xin's shifting kingdoms.

sentences.zh: 英布王淮南，彭越王梁也。」

translations.literal: Ying Bu was king of Huainan, and Peng Yue king of Liang."
translations.idiomatic: Ying Bu held Huainan while Peng Yue held Liang.

translations.idiomatic: Ying Shao, note 4: pronunciation gloss for "han" (ward).

sentences.zh: 盧綰與高祖同里，楚名里門為閈。

translations.literal: Lu Wan shared a neighborhood with the Supreme Ancestor; in Chu speech a ward gate is called han.
translations.idiomatic: Lu Wan grew up in the same lane as Liu Bang; Chu dialect called a lane gate a "han."

translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu cites Zuo zhuan to show the word was general, not regional slang.

translations.literal: Jia followed the campaigns with diligence and became bulwark of the Huai and Chu regions.
translations.idiomatic: Liu Jia, prince of Jing, served the Han armies with conspicuous effort and held the Huai-Chu sector firm.

translations.literal: [1] Prince Ze of Langya stirred the various Lüs with his maneuvering.
translations.idiomatic: Note 1: Liu Ze's enfeoffment in Langya helped trigger the backlash against the Lü clan.

translations.idiomatic: Note 2: Liu Bi's enlarged Wu fief ignored imperial limits; despite admonitions he rebelled and paid with execution.

translations.literal: [3] Narrating the Biographies of the Princes of Jing, Yan, and Wu, fifth.

translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu traces the phrase to the Changes.

translations.literal: The four sons of the Grand Supreme Emperor: Bo died in his youth; the house of Zhong was enfeoffed in Dai; Jiao took up his seat in Chu.
translations.idiomatic: Liu Taigong's four sons were Bo, who died young; Zhong, whose line held Dai; Gaozu, who founded the dynasty; and Jiao, first prince of Chu with his capital in the old Chu lands.

translations.literal: [2] Those who remained at the capital served generation after generation as director of the imperial clan; [3] they toiled for the royal house and were therefore enfeoffed at Yangcheng.
translations.idiomatic: Note 2: the Liu kindred who stayed in Chang'an became hereditary clan stewards; note 3: their service earned the Yangcheng marquisate.

translations.idiomatic: Note 4: Liu Xiang's erudition crowned three generations—hence the sixth summation, Prince Yuan of Chu.

sentences.zh: 〔一〕 師古曰：「詩衛風云『伯兮朅兮』，鄁風又曰『仲氏任只』。

translations.idiomatic: The quotations ornament the family prelude.

translations.literal: [2] Yan Shigu says: "Prince Wu of Chu committed adultery while in mourning for Empress Dowager Bo; the eastern sea commandery was stripped from him, so he joined Wu in rebellion and was executed.
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu, note 2: Liu Wu's incestuous breach of mourning law cost him territory and drove him into Liu Bi's revolt.

sentences.zh: 景帝更立平陸侯禮，續元王之後也。」

translations.literal: Emperor Jing then installed Marquis Pinglu, Liu Li, to continue the line of Prince Yuan."
translations.idiomatic: Jingdi replaced him with Liu Li of Pinglu to preserve Prince Yuan's descent line.

translations.literal: [3] Yan Shigu says: "Zheng, for rhyme, is read like zheng (march)."
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu, note 3: the character zheng here rhymes as zheng, the word for a military expedition.

sentences.zh: 〔四〕 師古曰：「謂劉德、劉向、劉歆，俱有名聞。」

translations.literal: [4] Yan Shigu says: "It refers to Liu De, Liu Xiang, and Liu Xin, all of whom enjoyed renown."
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu, note 4: three generations of the Liu scholars earned lasting fame.

sentences.zh: 季氏之詘，辱身毀節，信于上將，議臣震栗。

translations.literal: When Ji Bu was brought low—debasing his person and destroying his integrity—still he spoke truth to the commander-in-chief, and the debating ministers trembled.
translations.idiomatic: Though Ji Bu had been broken to a bondsman's status, he confronted Fan Kuai's rash war plan, and the whole faction of advisers shook with fear.

sentences.zh: 〔一〕欒公哭梁，田叔殉趙，見危授命，誼動明主。

translations.literal: [1] Luan Bu wept for Liang; Tian Shu died for Zhao; seeing peril they handed over their lives, and their righteousness moved the enlightened ruler.
translations.idiomatic: Note 1: Luan Bu mourned his former kingdom of Liang; Tian Shu followed Zhao king to the grave—each surrendered life for loyalty and stirred the throne.

sentences.zh: 布歷燕、齊，叔亦相魯，民思其政，或金或社。

translations.literal: Luan Bu campaigned through Yan and Qi; Tian Shu also served as minister to Lu; the people remembered their governance with gifts of metal or altars in their honor.
translations.idiomatic: Luan Bu's armies ranged the northeast while Tian Shu ruled Lu; Lu sent gold to Tian Shu's bier and Qi raised a living shrine to Luan Bu.

translations.literal: [2] Narrating the Biographies of Ji Bu, Luan Bu, and Tian Shu, seventh.
translations.idiomatic: Note 2: summation of the seventh grouped biography—Ji Bu, Luan Bu, and Tian Shu.

translations.idiomatic: Zhang Yan, note 1: the remonstrance was aimed at the commander-in-chief.

sentences.zh: 上將，樊噲也，欲以十萬眾橫行匈奴中，布曰：『噲可斬也。

translations.literal: The senior general was Fan Kuai, who wished to lead a hundred thousand men on a rampage through the Xiongnu; Bu said, 'Kuai deserves execution.'
translations.idiomatic: Fan Kuai boasted of a reckless northern campaign; Ji Bu answered that such talk merited the headsman's axe.

translations.literal: At the time every counselor was terrified.
translations.idiomatic: The whole faction of advisers fell silent in dread.

translations.literal: " Yan Shigu says: "Xin is to be read as shen, meaning 'to press' or 'declare.'"
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu: the graph read "xin" here means "to press" (shen).

sentences.zh: 〔二〕 李奇曰：「魯人愛田叔，死，送之以金。

translations.literal: [2] Li Qi says: "The people of Lu loved Tian Shu; when he died they sent him off with gifts of gold.
translations.idiomatic: Li Qi, note 2: Lu mourners weighed his coffin with gold offerings.

translations.literal: Qi honored Luan Bu and raised a living shrine to him."
translations.idiomatic: Qi set up a cult altar to Luan Bu while he still lived.

translations.literal: The Supreme Ancestor had eight sons—two became emperors and six became kings.
translations.idiomatic: Gaozu fathered eight princes: two ascended the throne and six received kingdoms.

sentences.zh: 三趙不辜，淮厲自亡，燕靈絕嗣，齊悼特昌。

translations.literal: The three Zhao lines perished unjustly; the Huai king destroyed himself; the Yan line ended without heirs; only Prince Dao of Qi flourished exceptionally.
translations.idiomatic: Three Zhao fiefs were wiped out though guiltless; Liu Chang of Huainan brought ruin on himself; the Yan house died out; only Prince Fei's Qi line thrived.

sentences.zh: 掩有東土，自岱徂海，支庶分王，前後九子。

translations.literal: They covered the eastern lands from Mount Dai to the sea; cadet branches were enfeoffed as kings—nine sons in all, earlier and later.
translations.idiomatic: Their sway ran from Taishan to the coast, with nine royal sons enfeoffed across generations.

translations.literal: When the six states were executed and destroyed, it fell to Qi alone to lose its sacrifices.
translations.idiomatic: The feudal purge ended every rival line, but Qi was the kingdom whose ancestral worship finally failed.

translations.literal: Chengyang and Jinbei afterward inherited our dynastic altars.
translations.idiomatic: Only the Chengyang and Beihai marquisates carried Prince Fei's blood into later Han.

translations.literal: [1] Fierce and bold was King Jing of Qi, who rescued the altars of Han.
translations.idiomatic: Note 1: Prince Zhang of Qi stood like a bulwark for the Liu house during the Lü crisis.

translations.literal: [2] Narrating the Biography of the Five Princes of Gaozu, eighth.
translations.idiomatic: Note 2: summation of the eighth treatise—Gaozu's five princely lines.

sentences.zh: 〔一〕 張晏曰：「濟北王志，吳楚反後徙王菑川。

translations.literal: [1] Zhang Yan says: "Prince Zhi of Jinbei was moved to be king of Zichuan after the Wu-Chu rebellion.
translations.idiomatic: Zhang Yan, note 1: Liu Zhi transferred from Beihai to Zichuan once the revolt ended.

sentences.zh: 元朔中，齊國絕，悼惠王後唯有城陽、菑川，武帝乃割臨菑環悼惠王冢，以與菑川，令奉祀也。

translations.literal: In the Yuanshuo era Qi was extinguished as a kingdom; among Prince Daohui's posterity only Chengyang and Zichuan remained, so Emperor Wu carved out the land around Linzi encircling the prince's tomb and attached it to Zichuan so sacrifices could continue.
translations.idiomatic: When central Qi was abolished, Wudi ring-fenced the tombs of Prince Fei with new territory granted to Zichuan so the line could still tend the grave.

translations.literal: " Yan Shigu says: "Shi is to be read as di, meaning legitimate heir."
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu: "shi" means the legitimate succession.

sentences.zh: 〔二〕 師古曰：「赳赳，武貌，音糾。」

translations.literal: [2] Yan Shigu says: "Jiu jiu describes a martial bearing, read like jiu."
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu, note 2: "jiu jiu" paints a warrior's stride.

sentences.zh: 猗與元勳，包漢舉信，〔一〕鎮守關中，足食成軍，營都立宮，定制修文。

translations.literal: Ah, the founding pillar—he embraced Han and raised Han Xin; [1] he guarded the passes within Guanzhong, stored grain to complete the army, built the capital and palaces, fixed institutions and polished the civil arts.
translations.idiomatic: Xiao He secured the heartland, fed the armies, raised Chang'an, and set the bureaucratic mold that made Han a state.

sentences.zh: 平陽玄默，繼而弗革，〔二〕民用作歌，化我淳德。

translations.literal: Pingyang was silent and deep, continuing without change; [2] the people made songs of it, and his pure virtue transformed us.
translations.idiomatic: Cao Can kept Xiao He's quiet governance; the folk sang his praise for preserving untroubled rule.

translations.literal: He was the dynastic bulwark of Han—this is what is called the chancellor of state.
translations.idiomatic: These were the true minister-clansmen on whom the empire rested.

translations.literal: Narrating the Biographies of Xiao He and Cao Can, ninth.
translations.idiomatic: Summation of the ninth paired biography—Xiao He and Cao Can.

translations.idiomatic: Zhang Liang's blow at Bolangsha prefaced a career of stratagem: feints at Wuguan and rescue at Hongmen saved Liu Bang.

translations.idiomatic: Chen Ping's defection stabilized Liu Bang; his ruses drove Fan Zeng to his death, broke Xiang Yu, freed Gaozu at Pingcheng, and lured Han Xin to capture—the six coups that left the throne unshaken.

translations.literal: [6] Wang Ling disputed in the court hall and then retired, barring his gate.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Ling defied the Lüs in open session and withdrew to shut his doors rather than bend.

translations.idiomatic: Zhou Bo purged the Lü clan and enthroned Wendi.

translations.literal: Yafu kept his integrity and earned merit against Wu and Chu.
translations.idiomatic: Zhou Yafu's iron discipline broke the eastern rebellion.

translations.idiomatic: Summation of the tenth grouped biography—the strategists and the Zhou marquises.

translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu unpacks the Wuguan stratagem: feints, bribes, and the sudden strike on a lax garrison.

translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu, note 4: fanqie for "rang" (turmoil).

translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu, note 5: "routing Di" is the stratagem that freed Gaozu at Pingcheng.

translations.idiomatic: "Seizing Han" is the pretended outing that caught Han Xin.

translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu, note 6: "wang" negates—"we had no hardship."

sentences.zh: 舞陽鼓刀，滕公廄騶，〔一〕潁陰商販，曲周庸夫，攀龍附鳳，並乘天衢。

translations.literal: Wuyang wheted the knife; Lord Teng was a stable groom; [1] Yingyin was a peddler, Quzhou a hireling—yet they climbed the dragon and clung to the phoenix, all mounting heaven's highway.
translations.idiomatic: Fan Kuai the dog-butcher, Xiahou Ying the carriage hand, Guan Ying the trader, and Zhou Xie the laborer rose with Liu Bang to share the conqueror's road.

sentences.zh: 〔二〕述樊酈滕灌傅靳周傳第十一。

translations.literal: [2] Narrating the Biographies of Fan, Li, Teng, Guan, Fu, Jin, and Zhou, eleventh.
translations.idiomatic: Note 2: summation of the eleventh grouped biography—the early military companions.

sentences.zh: 〔一〕 師古曰：「鼓刀謂屠狗也。」

translations.literal: [1] Yan Shigu says: "Gu dao means butchering dogs."
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu, note 1: "whetting the knife" means Fan Kuai's dog-meat trade.

translations.literal: [2] Yan Shigu says: "Cheng means to ascend."
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu, note 2: "cheng" is "to mount" or "rise."

sentences.zh: 北平志古，司秦柱下，〔一〕定漢章程，律度之緒。

translations.literal: Beiping loved antiquity and presided over Qin's pillar archives; [1] he fixed Han's statutes and regulations—the thread of law and measure.
translations.idiomatic: Zhang Cang drew on Warring States precedents to codify Han weights, measures, and written law.

translations.literal: The Marquis of Jiancheng was blunt and honest, offending superiors and daring the ruler's glance;
translations.idiomatic: Zhou Chang of Jiancheng spoke straight to Gaozu's face when law required it.

translations.literal: [2] at Guang'e he showed diligence and feasted on his old virtue.
translations.idiomatic: Zhao Yao earned his fief at Guang'e by steadfast service.

sentences.zh: 〔三〕故安執節，責通請錯，蹇蹇帝臣，匪躬之故。

translations.literal: [3] Gu'an grasped the tally, rebuked Deng Tong and demanded Chao Cuo's death—such kingly ministers, laboring not for private ends.
translations.idiomatic: Shentu Jia upheld the rod against favorites and demanded the execution of Chao Cuo for the realm's good.

sentences.zh: 〔四〕述張周趙任申屠傳第十二。

translations.literal: [4] Narrating the Biographies of Zhang Cang, Zhou Chang, Zhao Yao, Ren Ao, and Shentu Jia, twelfth.
translations.idiomatic: Note 4: summation of the twelfth grouped biography—the early chancellors and jurists.

translations.idiomatic: "Si" means he directed the archives under Qin.

translations.idiomatic: He cites the Changes: "feasting on old merit" describes Zhao Yao's reward.

translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu quotes the Jian hexagram on selfless ministers.

translations.idiomatic: Shentu Jia's summons of Deng Tong and demand for Chao Cuo's head match that oracle.

sentences.zh: 食其監門，長揖漢王，畫襲陳留，進收敖倉，塞隘杜津，王基以張。

translations.literal: Yiji kept the gate and bowed long to the King of Han; he plotted a surprise on Chenliu, advanced to seize Aocang, blocked defiles and sealed the fords, and the king's foundation thereby spread wide.
translations.idiomatic: Li Yiji opened Chenliu and the granaries, choking enemy supply lines so Liu Bang's enterprise could widen.

sentences.zh: 〔一〕賈作行人，百越來賓，從容風議，博我以文。

translations.literal: [1] Jia served as envoy until the hundred Yue came as guests; with calm ease he aired counsel and broadened us with pattern.
translations.idiomatic: Lu Jia's missions south brought tribute states to court and his New Conversations enriched the court's rhetoric.

sentences.zh: 〔二〕敬繇役夫，遷京定都，〔三〕內強關中，外和匈奴。

translations.literal: [2] Jing rose from corvée labor to move the capital and fix the seat; [3] within he strengthened Guanzhong, without he harmonized the Xiongnu.
translations.idiomatic: Liu Jing turned garrison duty into policy: Chang'an as capital, the heartland fortified, and marriage peace on the steppe.

sentences.zh: 叔孫奉常，與時抑揚，稅介免冑，禮義是創。

translations.literal: Shusun became chamberlain for ceremonials, bending with the times, doffing armor and helm—he was the founder of our rites and duties.
translations.idiomatic: Shusun Tong staged court etiquette so the rough conquerors could play emperor.

translations.literal: [4] Some pondered, some plotted, beholding the radiance of the state.
translations.idiomatic: Note 4: wise planners read the omens of dynastic greatness.

sentences.zh: 〔五〕述酈陸朱婁叔孫傳第十三。

translations.literal: [5] Narrating the Biographies of Li Yiji, Lu Jia, Zhu Jian, Lou Jing, and Shusun Tong, thirteenth.
translations.idiomatic: Note 5: summation of the thirteenth grouped biography—the rhetoricians and ritual architects.

translations.idiomatic: Li Qi, note 2: Lu Jia's book New Conversations.

translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu ties the phrase to Confucius enriching Yan Hui.

translations.idiomatic: Liu Jing began as a border draftee who won a hearing at court.

translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu cites the Shijing on counsel.

translations.idiomatic: He adds the Changes line on reading a kingdom's glory.

translations.literal: Hence the two are joined in one saying."
translations.idiomatic: Ban Gu fuses ode and oracle into one compliment.

sentences.zh: 〔六〕 師古曰：「本傳作朱、劉，終書其賜姓也。

translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu, note 6: the text lists Zhu and Liu but closes with the bestowed imperial surname.

translations.idiomatic: The verse uses their birth surnames Zhu and Lou.

translations.literal: Huainan acted the usurper in madness, and his two sons suffered disaster.
translations.idiomatic: Liu An's treason doomed his house and his heirs.

sentences.zh: 安辯而邪，賜頑以荒，敢行稱亂，窘世薦亡。

translations.literal: An was eloquent yet perverse; Ci was obstinate unto ruin—they dared call themselves rebels and, shaming their age, perished one after another.
translations.idiomatic: Liu An's sophistry masked treason while Liu Ci's obstinacy wasted him; each claimed kingship unlawfully and died in turn, disgracing their times.

sentences.zh: 〔一〕述淮南衡山濟北傳第十四。

translations.literal: [1] Narrating the Biographies of the Princes of Huainan, Hengshan, and Jinbei, fourteenth.
translations.idiomatic: Note 1: summation of the fourteenth grouped biography—the southern rebel princes.

translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu, note 1: the word jiong implies disaster arriving again and again in a single house.

translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu's gloss: the graph is read jian, indicating repeated disaster.

translations.idiomatic: The word marks calamity recurring in the same lineage.

translations.literal: Liu Chang died at Yong, and his son An afterward killed himself as well."
translations.idiomatic: The Huainan king perished in exile at Yong, and Liu An later took his own life in the same train of ruin.

sentences.zh: 蒯通壹說，三雄是敗，覆酈驕韓，田橫顛沛。

translations.literal: With a single persuasion Kuai Tong brought down three champions—he overturned Li Yiji's mission, fed Han Xin's arrogance, and left Tian Heng driven from pillar to post.
translations.idiomatic: One counselor's tongue toppled three titans: Qi swallowed Li Yiji alive, Han Xin overreached on his advice, and Tian Heng died a fugitive lord.

translations.literal: Once Wu Bei was bound in fetters, it turned into catastrophe.
translations.idiomatic: Imprisoning Wu Bei only pushed him toward the plot that destroyed the house.

translations.literal: [1] Jiang Chong and Xifu Gong knew no limit to slander; they threw the realm into vast disorder.
translations.idiomatic: Note 1: the two informers spread boundless calumny until the court reeled.

translations.literal: [2] Narrating the Biographies of Kuai Tong, Wu Bei, Jiang Chong, and Xifu Gong, fifteenth.
translations.idiomatic: Note 2: summation of the fifteenth grouped biography—the persuaders and slanderers.

sentences.zh: 〔一〕 師古曰：「言伍被初不從王反，王繫其父母，乃進邪謀，終以遇害也。」

translations.literal: [1] Yan Shigu says: "It means that at first Wu Bei would not follow the king in revolt; the king imprisoned his parents, whereupon he offered wicked counsel and in the end perished for it."
translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu explains Wu Bei's forced turn to treason after the king seized his kin.

sentences.zh: 〔二〕 師古曰：「小雅青蠅之詩云『讒言罔極，交亂四國』。

translations.literal: [2] Yan Shigu says: "The 'Green Flies' ode in the Minor Odes reads, 'Slander knows no limit; it throws the four states into confusion.'
translations.idiomatic: He cites the Shijing on rumor that poisons kingdoms.

sentences.zh: 此敘言江充、息夫躬之惡，引以為辭也。」

translations.literal: This passage narrates the evil of Jiang Chong and Xifu Gong and borrows that line as its tag."
translations.idiomatic: Ban Gu applies the ode to the witchcraft persecutions.

sentences.zh: 萬石溫溫，幼寤聖君，〔一〕宜爾子孫，夭夭伸伸，〔二〕慶社于齊，不言動民。

translations.literal: The Wan Shi house was mild and warm; in youth he moved the sage ruler; [1] may your sons and grandsons thrive, gentle and at ease; [2] Qing won a shrine in Qi without boastful claims of swaying the people.
translations.idiomatic: Shi Fen's clan rose on modest virtue: the emperor noticed the boy's gravity, his descendants multiplied in harmony, and Shi Qing earned Qi worship without self-advertisement.

translations.literal: [3] Wei, Zhi, Zhou, and Zhang kept themselves with careful goodness.
translations.idiomatic: Note 3: the four younger ministers matched the family's scruple.

sentences.zh: 〔四〕述萬石衛直周張傳第十六。

translations.literal: [4] Narrating the Biographies of the Wan Shi Clan, Wei Wan, Zhi Buyi, Zhou Ren, and Zhang Ou, sixteenth.
translations.idiomatic: Note 4: summation of the sixteenth grouped biography—the Wan Shi line and allies.

translations.idiomatic: The clan's boys won Gaozu's favor through grave manners while still young.

translations.idiomatic: Yan Shigu piles classical parallels on the family's fertility and calm.

translations.idiomatic: The verses praise a crowded, peaceable household.

translations.idiomatic: Deng Zhan, note 3: Qi's living shrine to Shi Qing.

translations.idiomatic: The quotation honors the four ministers named in the verse.

sentences.zh: 孝文三王，代孝二梁，〔一〕懷折亡嗣，孝乃尊光。

translations.literal: The three princely sons of Emperor Wen—Prince Xiao of Dai and the two Liang princes, Xiao and Huai; [1] Huai died young without heirs, and Xiao's line alone grew glorious.
translations.idiomatic: Wendi's three royal boys: Dai and two Liang fiefs; the younger Liang line failed while the elder Liang house flourished.

sentences.zh: 〔二〕內為母弟，外扞吳楚，怙寵矜功，僭欲失所，思心既霿，牛禍告妖。

translations.literal: [2] Within the palace they were the emperor's younger brothers; without, they shielded the realm from Wu and Chu; trusting in favor and boasting of merit, they overreached until they lost their footing; once their hearts grew murky with presumption, ox omens announced portents.
translations.idiomatic: Note 2: royal brothers who defended the east yet swaggered on imperial love until omens and bovine prodigies warned of doom.

sentences.zh: 〔三〕帝庸親親，厥國五分，〔四〕德不堪寵，四支不傳。
